acceptable.choice: Keep delivery in Ruby/Sidekiq, but move webhooks to their own queue and their own ECS service, autoscaled on queue latency
acceptable.why: The work is I/O-bound waiting on slow customer servers, so the fix is more concurrent requests in flight, which Ruby threads handle well because the GVL is released during network I/O, and the team already knows how to run this.

acceptable.choice: Per-endpoint isolation in Ruby: per-customer concurrency limits, circuit breakers, and a separate slow/retry lane for failing or slow endpoints (Sidekiq Enterprise limiters or Redis-based limits)
acceptable.why: The hours-long backlog is mostly head-of-line blocking: a few slow customers tie up every worker for 5 s each, and isolating them frees capacity for everyone else.

acceptable.choice: Split payload building from delivery: a Rails job renders and stores the payload, and a thin delivery job only does the HTTP POST using a persistent-connection client and no DB connection
acceptable.why: This keeps the Postgres connection pool and the monolith safe as delivery concurrency grows into the hundreds or thousands.

acceptable.choice: Fiber-based concurrent delivery in Ruby (async / async-http) inside a dedicated webhook worker
acceptable.why: One process can hold hundreds to thousands of in-flight POSTs, which covers the peak concurrency without a new language.
It takes over retries, per-endpoint backoff, signing and a customer-facing delivery log, which helps both product velocity and quiet on-call, provided cost and data-handling terms are acceptable.

acceptable.choice: A small Go delivery service later, owned by the platform team, but only if measured Ruby fixes still fall short
acceptable.why: It is a reasonable escalation path because the team already writes Go, but it should follow the cheap fixes, not replace them.

ruled_out.choice: An immediate Go rewrite as the main fix
ruled_out.why: It does not touch the real bottleneck (concurrency and slow endpoints, not CPU speed), it moves a customer-facing system onto a 3-person team that would then carry its on-call, and it is slower to ship than the Ruby fixes.

ruled_out.choice: Just adding more Sidekiq threads or processes to the shared queue
ruled_out.why: Without endpoint isolation, slow customers still take over the extra capacity, the extra threads can exhaust Postgres connections, and other Sidekiq jobs keep competing with webhooks.

ruled_out.choice: Kafka, Kubernetes, or a new event-streaming platform
ruled_out.why: At ~23/s on average (a few hundred per second at peak) this is heavy operational overhead that works against quiet on-call and against their ECS/Terraform setup.

ruled_out.choice: Raising the timeout or dropping retries to clear the queue
ruled_out.why: A longer timeout makes worker starvation worse, and dropping retries breaks the delivery guarantee B2B customers rely on.

ruled_out.choice: Self-hosting a webhook gateway such as Convoy as a first step
ruled_out.why: It adds a new stateful system to operate, which costs more than fixing the existing Sidekiq path.

must_mention: Recommend fixing it in Ruby first; the language is not the bottleneck, time spent waiting on network I/O is.

Back-of-envelope with Little's law: ~2M/day is ~23/s on average and maybe 100–300/s at peak; with responses taking up to 5 s, that means hundreds to ~1,000+ requests in flight, a concurrency and isolation problem rather than a CPU one.
Slow or dead customer endpoints cause head-of-line blocking; add per-endpoint concurrency caps, circuit breakers and a separate retry/slow queue.
Give webhooks a dedicated queue and worker service so they cannot starve or be starved by other monolith jobs, and autoscale it on queue latency in ECS.
Keep DB connections out of the hot delivery path (pre-render payloads) so higher concurrency does not overwhelm Postgres.
Measure before deciding: per-endpoint latency distribution, timeout and error rates, peak rate, and current worker concurrency.
A Go service is a valid later option if the metrics justify it, but weigh the ownership and on-call cost for a 3-person platform team.
red_flags: Claiming Ruby is too slow or that the GVL makes concurrent HTTP impossible.
Recommending a rewrite without any capacity math or measurement.
Recommending more workers without isolating slow endpoints or checking the Postgres connection pool.
Proposing heavy infrastructure (Kafka, Kubernetes, service mesh) for a few hundred requests per second.
Weakening delivery guarantees (no retries, silently dropping events) or raising timeouts as the fix.
Ignoring who carries on-call and maintenance for a new Go service.
Recommending a third-party webhook SaaS without mentioning cost, data-handling or compliance review.
unknowns: Peak per-second rate and how bursty traffic is.
Response-time and failure distribution per customer endpoint (are a few endpoints causing most of the delay?).
Current Sidekiq concurrency, process count, and whether webhooks share a queue with other jobs.
Whether delivery jobs currently do DB queries or CPU-heavy payload rendering.
Delivery SLA, ordering requirements, and retry policy promised to customers.
Whether they have a Sidekiq Pro/Enterprise license, or budget and compliance clearance for a managed webhook service.
Postgres connection headroom and Redis memory under a large backlog.
